15

  • N: [š]akin | kibsu(m) | šutēšur | padānu(m)-ma | ... kibs[u(m)]
  • T: there is a track, the way is well trodden, … track.
  • L: [š]akin ← šakānu I “to put, place, lay down”; kibsu(m) ← kibsu I “pl. m. & f. track, footprint”; šutēšur ← ešēru I “to be/go well”; padānu(m)-ma ← padānu I “f. & m. way, path OAkk, Bab.”; kibs[u(m)] ← kibsu I “pl. m. & f. track, footprint”
  • Note: [RN117: 258]: “As van Dijk also noted, [these lines are] similar to a couplet of the late version: ašar Ḫumbāba ittallaku šakin kibsu / ḫarrānātu šutēšurāma ṭubbat girru (SB V 4–5). Here it is evidently direct speech, not narrative. At the end of l. 15 there may be dittography: ša#-ki!#-in!# ki#-ib#-s[u]? The spelling šu-te-ši-ir for the regular OB stative šutēšur finds a parallel in another literary tablet from Tell Harmal, the fable of Tamarisk and Date-Palm, in which the construct state of the infinitive is likewise rendered ([RN432: 155, IM 53946, 4]: [a-n]a šu-te-ši-ir ma-tim). An orthography attested twice over is more easily seen as a reflection of local pronunciation or dialect than as a spelling mistake. As Lambert points out ([RN432: 328]), the regular infinitive šu-te-šu-ur also occurs at Tell Harmal, in a bilingual excerpt of Inninšagurra (now TIM IX 21, 9, ed. [sjoeberg1975in-nin: 188, 118]).”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "V" 4; cf. L I.4 SB "V" 5
ŠadOB1 o 15. [š]a-ki-in ki-ib-su šu-te#-ši#-ir pa-da-nu-ma ša# na# x ki#-ib#-s[u]

16

  • L: [n]ittalka ← alāku I “to go”; aš(šu)ru ← ašru III “pl. m. & f., place, site”; lā ← lā I “not, no”; alākim ← alāku I “to go”; idka ← idu I “pl. m. & f. arm”
  • Note: [RN117: 258]: “The spelling aš-šu-ru for ašru can also be interpreted as local pronunciation. A similar expansion may happen in the OB incantation TIM IX 66, 4: aš-šu-nu-gal-lam // 65, 2: aš-nu-ga-la-am (both ed. [RN2226: 226]), where the word aš(šu)nugallum refers to a snake.”
ŠadOB1 o 16. [n]e-ta-al-ka aš-šu-ru la a-la-ki-im id-ka [x] x x

17

  • N: i niškun | kakka | ina bāb (|) huwāwa | ... [ ... ]
  • T: Let us set a weapon in the gate of Huwawa! …’
  • L: i ← i I “let's”; niškun ← šakānu I “to put, place, lay down”; kakka ← kakku I “stick”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; bāb ← bābu I “pl. m. & f. gate, door”; huwāwa ← Humbaba I
  • Note: [RN117: 258]: “The sequence i niškun kakka ina bāb Ḫuwāwa makes for a line of poetry as it stands, but the passage is so broken it is impossible to be absolutely sure that the verb and the locative phrase belong together. However, kakkam šakānum makes good sense as a suitably symbolic act. See also the OB Sargon tale from Tell Harmal (TIM IX 48), where the clause iš-ku-un ka-ki-šu (i 13'), ‘he set in place his weapons’, describes one of the things that Sargon did after taking possession of the Cedar Forest. Westenholz translates, ‘readied his weapons’ ([RN262: 82]), but a symbolic interpretation is suggested by the following clauses, i-ta-qí ni-qí-šu il-bi-in ap-pa-šu, ‘he made his sacrifices, he paid homage’. The three actions can be understood in the context as ritual acts marking Sargon’s conquest of the territory and his thanksgiving to the divine power or powers that made it possible. What Gilgameš and Enkidu intend to do is to mark their conquest of Huwawa’s domain.”
ŠadOB1 o 17. i# ni#-iš#-ku-un ka?#-ka i-na ba-a-ba hu-bi-bi x di x [(x)]

18

  • N: [ ... ] ... ilqe ... | (w)ašṭu? | ša ṣēri
  • T: […] … took … The fierce one of the wild
  • L: ilqe ← leqû II “to take, take over”; (w)ašṭu? ← ašṭu I “stiff, difficult Bab.”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ṣēri ← ṣēru I “back, upperside”
  • Note: [RN117: 258]: “The phrase ...-tu ša ṣērim is evidently an epithet of Enkidu, the subject of [issaqqar]am ana ibrīšu in the next line, and comparable with waldam ṣērim (l. 47). None of the synonyms for ‘offspring’ seems to fit the traces. Provisionally I assume that the signs aš-ṭú (i.e., wašṭum) are the result of a misunderstanding of waldum in the light of the phonetic development š+dental > l+dental, already well attested in OB in the noun iltānum < ištānum, ‘north wind, north’ (CAD I, p. 269, 1d1'; GAG³ §30g*).”
ŠadOB1 o 18. [x x x] x-bi-a-tum il-qe₂ x x x aš-ṭu₂ ša ṣe₂-ri

37

  • N: ... | ikrubūš | pānam | ana melammī | ištakan | ... [ ... ] ...
  • T: … greeted him, he turned his gaze to the radiant auras, to smite
  • L: ikrubūš ← karābu II “to pray, bless, greet”; pānam ← pānu I “front, pl. face”; ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; melammī ← melemmu I “mostly pl. fearsome radiance, aura Bab.(lit.) of deity, demon”; ištakan ← šakānu I “to put, place, lay down”
  • Note: [RN117: 258]: “Van Dijk read [inū]mi ikrubušši, ‘lorsqu’il l’eut prié’, and, identifying obverse and reverse differently from me, saw the context as Gilgameš’s prayer to Ninsun earlier in the story (cf. SB III 23 ff.). Room for i-nu-mi is lacking, however, and the traces are also against it. The form ikrubušši is not a viable one; ikrubu-š is good hymno-epic style, leaving ŠI to be explained separately. At the end Van Dijk read ši-[pí]-šu, ‘il dirigea ses pas’, but the new copy casts doubt on this. My understanding is that the object of ištakan has already been expressed, as pānam(igi).”

38

  • N: ana hatāʾim | balāṭam-ma | ul balṭānu | gilgāmeš [ ... ] ...
  • T: its … ‘We are not truly alive, O Gilgameš, …
  • L: ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; balāṭam-ma ← balāṭu I “life esp. ana balāṭ X for X's life”; ul ← ul I “not Bab., to negate main clause”; balṭānu ← balāṭu I “life esp. ana balāṭ X for X's life”; gilgāmeš ← Gilgameš I
  • Note: [RN117: 258–259]: “Use of the sign HI for ṭà is typical of Mari orthography but occurs also at Tell Harmal and elsewhere in the Diyala basin (see [RN262: 80]). It can be seen as diagnostic of the Diyala tradition. The phrase balāṭamma ul balṭānu is clearly an example of a paronomastic infinitive construction, but an exceptional one in this period. There are very few examples of the accusative singular of the paronomastic infinitive in OB, three being noted by [stol1976studies: 105]; this, the fourth, is the first with enclitic -ma. OB paronomastic infinitives with -ma otherwise follow the model parāsumma, which Aro and von Soden analyse as locative (see [RN776: 112–13, 4.8]; GAG³ §150a*). The only other example of parāsamma is very late, in Erra IV 112: na-ha-am-ma ul ta-nu-uh, ‘you found no peace at all’.”
ŠadOB1 r 10. a#-na ha-ta-im ba-la-ṭam₂-ma u₂#-ul ba-al-ṭa₃-nu {d}bi[l₄ x] x x-nam?

42

  • N: ulidka | littum || ša supūri | ninsumuna
  • T: The cow of the fold, the goddess Ninsun, bore you!
  • L: ulidka ← alādu I “to give birth (to)”; littum ← lītu II “pl. liātu, lâtu cow”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; supūri ← supūru I “sheepfold Bab.(lit.) for sheep and goats”; ninsumuna ← Ninsun I
  • Note: [RN117: 259]: “Or ‘folds’. These words parallel those with which Ḫumbaba acknowledges Gilgameš’s divine origin at this point in the later text (SB V <168>): u ilitti ša [Rīmat-Ninsun] atta, and echo more closely still Enkidu’s acceptance of Gilgameš’s royal status at the end of the Pennsylvania tablet: kīma ištēnma ummaka ūlidka / rīmtum ša supūrim (or supūrī) Ninsunna (OB II 234–7). For the long form of the goddess’s name see Chapter 4, the section on Ninsun.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 OB "II" 234-235; cf. L I.4 SB "V" 168

46

  • N: luṣṣurkku(m) | erēnam | šurmēnam | supālam | šīhūt[im | iṣṣ]ī
  • T: Let me keep for you cedar, cypress and *supālu-*juniper, the tallest trees
  • L: luṣṣurkku(m) ← naṣāru I “to guard, protect”; erēnam ← erēnu I “cedar OAkk qišti e. cedar forest”; šurmēnam ← šurmēnu I “cypress as tree, timber”; supālam ← supālu I “(a) juniper OAkk, O/jB”; šīhūt[im ← šīhu I “grown (tall) Bab., NA of gods, men, physique”; iṣṣ]ī ← iṣu I “pl. m. iṣṣū, OA also f. tree”
  • Note: The new reading luṣṣurkku(m) seems compatible with the copy [ARG]. See [RN117: 259]: “(…). The three trees mentioned here occur together in Sumerian literature as sources of timber for grand building-projects: {gišeren {giš}šu.ur₂.min₃ {giš}za.ba.lum {giš}taškarin} (Curse of Akkade 134); {gišeren {giš}šu.ur₂.me {giš}za.ba.lum} (Gudea Cyl. A xii 5). In Akkadian note Mt Ḫašur as šad {giš}erēni(eren) bi-šit {giš}erēni(eren) {giš}šurmēni(šur.mìn) {giš}ši-qit-ti {giš}su-pa-li, ‘mountain of cedar, place of origin(?) of cedar, cypress, almond, supālu-juniper, etc.’ (BBR 75 obv. 6–7; SB divination prayer). The phrase šīḫūtim iṣṣī simātu ēkallim is reminiscent of the passage of the late text in which Ḫumbaba, pleading for his life, promises to reserve various kinds of timber for his conqueror (SB V 154–5): luṣṣurka asa […] / iṣṣī bālti ēkal[li …]. The reversing of the usual order of noun and adjective probably stresses the latter: see Chapter 9, the section on Some features of language and style.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 MB "Ug₂" b+12; cf. L I.4 SB "V" 176
ŠadOB1 r 18. [l]u-ṣu₂-ur₂!-ku {giš}EREN {giš}ŠU.UR₂.MIN₃ {giš#}su#-pa-lam ši-hu-t[im i-ṣ]i₂

47

  • N: [s]imatu (|) ēkalli | waldam (|) ṣērim || mitlukam | ileʾʾi
  • T: fit to decorate a palace!’ The wild-born was able to give counsel:
  • L: [s]imatu ← simtu I “appropriate symbol, characteristic before abstr. nouns symbol, proper…”; ēkalli ← ēkallu I “f., rarely m.”; waldam ← waldu I “born OA, OB, M/jB”; ṣērim ← ṣēru I “back, upperside”; mitlukam ← malāku II “to discuss”; ileʾʾi ← le'û I “to be able, powerful”
  • Note: [RN117: 259]: “The last four words recur in OB IM 19 and can be identified as a stock line. The phrase waldam ṣērim can be added to the list of phrases that use this construction, as studied by [reiner1984damqam: 175–82 (Type 3)]. This line is an older version of the line and a half which conclude at least two dream episodes in SB IV (26–7: [š]a iʾʾaldamma ina ṣ[ēri mitluka ileʾʾi] / [iza]kkara ana ibrīšu, 107: [taʾʾald]amma ina ṣēri mitluka nileʾʾ[i]). Another variant occurs in OB Harmal₂ 18–19.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "IV" 26; cf. L I.4 SB "IV" 107; cf. L I.4 SB "V" 177; cf. L I.4 OB "IM" 19; cf. L I.4 MB "Ug₂" c+7
